title: PRD look
subtitle: Five ways a PRD reads, section to section (invented PRD; re-snap with real PRDs on your laptop, see README)

decisions.name: PRD look
decisions.question: How should a PRD read, section to section?
decisions.common: Every proposal keeps the same content, the toolbar, the version header, the review panel and every section action (⋯ menu, Edit, Refine, review bar, comments). Each works on every PRD as written, with no regeneration. Feature codes open the feature panel; citations show as chips.

proposals.name: Calm document
proposals.what: One readable column about 720 px wide on a white sheet. Every section has a number (1, 2, 10.4, 11.7), a rule and generous space above it, and a larger heading; body text is set a size up with more line height. A contents rail on the left stays in view, lights the section being read and shows each section's review state as a dot. The review bar shows on the section being read; every other section shows only its ⋯ menu.
proposals.why: It fixes what makes a PRD hard to read today, the lack of space and landmarks between sections, without moving anything people already know: the toolbar, the version header, the review panel and every section action stay where they are. It needs no change to the template and works on every PRD as written, and the PDF can take the same numbers and rules in a few lines.
proposals.plus: Calm and fast to scan; numbers make sections easy to name in a review ("see 10.4"); the lit rail shows where you are in a 50-section PRD.
proposals.cost: At 1440 the rail cuts long feature names short, the 720 px column makes the widest table scroll across at 1512 and 1440, and the review bar shows only on the section being read. Template file: no change (numbers come from the heading levels). PDF (prd.html.j2): add the section numbers and the rule and space between sections; about 20 lines of CSS.

proposals.name: Section cards
proposals.what: Each section is a card. Its header bar carries the number, title and ⋯ menu, and a line under it the owner, review state and the version it last changed in. The review bar sits at the foot of every card. Sub-sections nest as inner cards. A Sections strip at the top stays in view and opens the contents.
proposals.plus: Owner, state and last change are on every section without opening anything; review work reads like a list of cards to clear.
proposals.cost: Cards take more height: fewer sections fit on a screen and a long PRD scrolls further. Template file: no change. PDF (prd.html.j2): each section boxed with a header line, which needs the owner and review state passed to the export.

proposals.name: Summary first
proposals.what: The PRD opens with a summary panel built from what the PRD already says: the goals with measure and target, the dates, the 20 features as code and name, and the review state. Below it the sections are grouped into parts (Why, What we build, When it ships, Risks and decisions, Sources) with a divider each; long sections are folded to their first lines with Show all.
proposals.plus: A reader gets the goal, dates and features in one screen before reading on; parts make the order of a long PRD clear.
proposals.cost: Folded sections take one more click to read in full, and the part a section belongs to has to be known. Template file: add a parts list to the front matter (like brief: today) naming which sections sit in which part. PDF (prd.html.j2): a summary page first and a divider per part; nothing folded in print.

proposals.name: Margin spec
proposals.what: Each section is a row: a left margin carries its number, owner, review state and the version it changed in, and the text sits on the right, like the one-pager's margin notes. A line down the margin marks the section being read. The contents rail on the left stays in view.
proposals.plus: Who owns a section and where it stands sit beside the text without breaking it; good for a review pass section by section.
proposals.cost: The margin takes about 180 px: the text column is narrower and the widest table must be scrolled across at 1512 and 1440. Template file: no change. PDF (prd.html.j2): a two-column layout per section, with wide tables spanning the full page.

proposals.name: Printed report
proposals.what: The PRD reads like the PDF: a page-wide paper sheet, a serif body, big section openers ("Section 12" over the title) with a heavy rule, and tables with a shaded header row. The web and the printed copy look the same.
proposals.plus: One look on screen and on paper; reads like a formal document for people outside the team.
proposals.cost: The sheet is narrower than the screen and the serif face is denser: the widest table wraps into tall rows, worst on a phone. Template file: no change. PDF (prd.html.j2): little to change, it already is this look; the web takes over its stylesheet.

decisions.name: PRD on the Simple side
decisions.question: How should a PRD read in Simple, from block to block and into its sections?
decisions.common: Every proposal keeps the one-pager as it is: each block and line, Edit and Propose, Needs a look, Start a review meeting, Export PDF, Present, the plan strip, the timeline, notes and statuses. Each also shows the PRD's own sections as written, with no regeneration; a feature code opens the same feature panel as everywhere in Simple. a, b, c and e are the Simple twins of PT1 a, b, c and e; d is Simple only.

proposals.name: Calm page
proposals.what: The one-pager as today, then the whole PRD under it in one calm column: every section numbered (1, 4, 11.7) with space and a rule between sections and body text a size up. A contents list on the left stays in view: the one-pager's blocks first, then the PRD's sections. A feature code at the start of a line becomes a small chip that opens the feature panel.
proposals.why: It is the Simple twin of PT1 a (Calm document): the same numbers, rules and spacing, so a person who moves between Simple and Detailed reads one product. Nothing on the one-pager moves; the PRD is simply there to read below it, as written.
proposals.plus: Reads top to bottom with no clicks; the contents list shows where you are and jumps to any section; section numbers match Detailed's.
proposals.cost: A long page: the whole PRD sits under the one-pager. Template: no change (numbers come from heading levels). One-pager read: the page also reads the PRD version the one-pager is built from (GET /v1/documents/{doc}/versions/{n}, one more request; the one-pager's own read is unchanged). PDF and slides: no change (the one-pager PDF and Present show the one-pager only).

proposals.name: Cards
proposals.what: Each one-pager block and each PRD section is a card with a header bar that names it ("Section 4"); cards sit on the page's tint with space between them. The One-pagers list is a grid of cards too.
proposals.why: The Simple twin of PT1 b (Section cards): each part is a clear box, easy to tell apart when scanning.
proposals.plus: Very clear where one part ends and the next starts; works well on a phone, one card under another.
proposals.cost: Cards take height: fewer sections fit on a screen, and there is no contents list. Template: no change. One-pager read: the page also reads the PRD version the one-pager is built from (GET /v1/documents/{doc}/versions/{n}, one more request; the one-pager's own read is unchanged). PDF and slides: no change (the PDF could draw the same boxes; not needed).

proposals.name: Summary first
proposals.what: A row of tiles over the page: the outcomes (18.4% to 12%, 41% to 95%), how many bets, how many risks and open decisions, and the first delivery date; each tile jumps to its block. Under the one-pager, the whole PRD in parts (Why, What we build, When it ships, Risks and decisions, Sources), long sections folded with Read all.
proposals.why: The Simple twin of PT1 c (Summary first): the numbers that matter in one glance, then the detail in an order that tells the story.
proposals.plus: A busy reader gets the goal, size and date before reading a line; parts make a long PRD easy to follow.
proposals.cost: Folded sections take one more click to read, and which part a section sits in has to be known (a list by section key; a key it does not know follows the section before it). Template: no change. One-pager read: the page also reads the PRD version the one-pager is built from (GET /v1/documents/{doc}/versions/{n}, one more request; the one-pager's own read is unchanged). PDF and slides: no change (the tiles could open the PDF's first page; not needed).

proposals.name: Questions
proposals.what: Each block asks its question: What problem are we solving, and for whom? What will we build? How will we know it worked? Under each answer, Read it in the PRD opens the sections it rests on. A list of the questions stays on the left; at the end, What else is in the PRD? lists every other section, each folded.
proposals.why: A Simple-only idea: a one-pager read as the questions people ask in a review, with the PRD's own words one click under each answer.
proposals.plus: Plain for people who do not know PRD terms; each answer leads to its proof in the PRD.
proposals.cost: The PRD is not read in its own order: sections are grouped under questions, the rest in a list of folds at the end; the questions are set per block. Template: no change (a block's questions are fixed in the page; the sections come from each line's sources). One-pager read: the page also reads the PRD version the one-pager is built from (GET /v1/documents/{doc}/versions/{n}, one more request; the one-pager's own read is unchanged). PDF and slides: block titles could become the questions; not needed.

proposals.name: Printed pages
proposals.what: The one-pager and the PRD as printed sheets on a desk: serif headings, thin rules and tables set small, as in the PDF. The PRD follows in pages by part (Page 2 Why, Page 3 What we build).
proposals.why: The Simple twin of PT1 e (Printed report): what you read on screen is what the PDF looks like.
proposals.plus: No surprise when the PDF is opened or printed; feels like a finished document to hand on.
proposals.cost: The PDF's small type: tables are set at 13 px to fit the sheet, harder to read on a screen; the sheets need a wide screen to look like paper. Template: no change. One-pager read: the page also reads the PRD version the one-pager is built from (GET /v1/documents/{doc}/versions/{n}, one more request; the one-pager's own read is unchanged). PDF: the one-pager PDF would take the same serif headings and rules (its template's CSS); slides: no change.
